title: Is Productive Struggle Ethical?
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman argues that productive struggle - asking students to wrestle with a problem before being taught how to solve it - is not just pedagogically weak but ethically indefensible for most maths classrooms. He traces the idea's lineage from constructivist theory through its recent rebrand as productive failure (Manu Kapur), and directly disputes a widely-shared 2021 meta-analysis by Sinha and Kapur that found in favour of the approach, noting he reviewed much of the same literature for his own PhD and reached the opposite conclusion. Ashman's methodological critique centres on the comparison conditions researchers use: to make explicit teaching look worse, studies often compare it to setups no real teacher would choose, undermining the ecological validity of pro-struggle findings. His core ethical argument is distributional - struggle-first approaches predictably disadvantage students with the least prior knowledge, who are least likely to succeed through unaided struggle, while a small group who land on the canonical solution get publicly held up as naturally talented, reinforcing rather than closing gaps. He closes by arguing that mitigating the harms of struggle with extra teacher guidance concedes the whole game - comparing it to intentionally holing a boat and then bailing water - and instead advocates equipping students with strategies up front so the inevitable struggles of learning maths don't become a reason to disengage from the subject.
points: Ashman traces productive struggle back to constructivist theory and its more recent rebrand as productive failure (Kapur), arguing each new name repackages the same contested claim that students must construct concepts through struggle rather than being told them.

Drawing on his own PhD literature review of the same meta-analysis Kapur and Sinha used, Ashman disputes the celebrated finding, noting the comparison conditions used to make explicit teaching look worse are often ecologically invalid setups no real teacher would choose.

His ethical objection is distributional: struggle-first pedagogy predictably fails hardest for the least-advantaged students, who have the fewest prior-knowledge resources to draw on, while the small group who solve problems the canonical way get held up as naturally good at maths.

Ashman's boat metaphor crystallizes his objection to mitigated productive struggle: giving students extra guidance to offset the harms of struggle is like drilling a hole in a boat and then bailing the water out, rather than not drilling the hole.
quotes: It is odd to think of teachers designing lessons with the intention of causing their students to struggle and yet this is a popular and pervasive idea, particularly in the world of mathematics teaching.
Productive failure involves setting students a problem that makes sense to them but for which they have not been taught the standard — or ‘canonical’ — solution method.
It is not by chance that when reviewing teacher effectiveness research, Barak Rosenshine noted that the more effective teachers obtain a high success rate.
Intentionally causing struggle and then mitigating the negative effects is like intentionally making a hole in the bottom of a row boat and then grabbing a bucket to bail out the water.
Most children learning maths do not need their teachers to intentionally cause them to struggle because they are going to struggle anyway with this weird, unnatural subject.
Given the foreseeable effects, intentionally causing struggle does not seem to be an ethical way to proceed.

Logically, those students who are the least advantaged and bring the fewest resources to a problem are the least likely to be successful when struggling, but it is precisely these students who need motivation, not those who are already advantaged.
